mainTopic: Proving ownership in court: witnesses who disagree, a buyer's חזקה through a middleman, and three buyers combining for a חזקה
overview: This amud has three parts. First, רב כהנא is sued before רב יהודה. One witness says he took two rows of his neighbor's land and the other says three, and רב יהודה rules that he must give back two. רב כהנא says this follows רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's reading of בית הלל, who join two witnesses who disagree for the smaller amount. He says a letter from ארץ ישראל rules against that view, and רב יהודה tells him to bring it first. Second, a man has lived in a house for four years and says he bought it from someone who bought it from the original owner. רבי חייא rules that he keeps it only if witnesses saw his seller living there, even for one day. רב asks about a quick resale, and the answer is that a buyer who says he saw the earlier sale is believed because of a מיגו. רבא tries to support רבי חייא from the משנה about an heir, but the גמרא rejects that proof two ways. אביי and רבא then argue whether just seeing the seller in the house is enough. Third, three buyers in a row can combine their years toward a חזקה, and רב says only if each bought with a שטר. The גמרא asks how this fits with another ruling of רב, that a sale before witnesses does become public, and the answer continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Witnesses disagree: two rows or three, and רב יהודה rules pay two
steps.stepSummary: A land case comes before רב יהודה. The two witnesses disagree on how much land was taken, and he rules that the overlapping amount must be paid.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא came before רב יהודה. His neighbor brought two witnesses. One said רב כהנא took in two rows of the neighbor's land, and the other said three rows. רב יהודה told him: Go pay two out of the three.
steps.whatsHappening: A court story: two witnesses give different numbers, and רב יהודה rules that רב כהנא must pay the smaller number that both witnesses agree on.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally you need two witnesses who say the same thing. Here they disagree, two rows versus three. רב יהודה treats the 'two' as something both witnesses are really saying, since whoever says three also agrees there were at least two. So he combines them for the smaller amount.

keyTerms.meaning: Rows (of planting or land) in a field

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling sets up the whole question of the passage: can two witnesses who disagree on the amount still be joined together for the amount they share?

phrases.english: He came before Rav Yehuda.
phrases.notes: The one who came is רב כהנא, from the story just before this.

phrases.english: He went and brought two witnesses.
phrases.notes: This 'he' is the neighbor who is suing רב כהנא.

phrases.english: One said: he entered two rows,
and one said: he entered three rows.
He said to him: Go pay
two out of the three.
phrases.notes: He means give back the two rows that both witnesses agree on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the story of רב כהנא's court case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When two witnesses disagree on the amount (two rows versus three), they are combined for the smaller shared amount, so two rows must be paid.

steps.title: רב כהנא asks whose opinion this ruling follows
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא asks רב יהודה what his ruling is based on and suggests רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said to him: Whose opinion are you following? רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's?
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא asks where רב יהודה's ruling comes from and guesses רבי שמעון בן אלעזר. This sets up the source he is about to quote.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Joining two witnesses who disagree is not obvious, so רב כהנא wants to know who allows it. By tying the ruling to one specific תנא, he prepares to attack it later if the הלכה does not follow that תנא.

keyTerms.meaning: According to whom? (Whose opinion is this?)
A תנא whose ברייתא is about to be quoted

phrases.english: He said to him: In accordance with whom?
Like Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source behind רב יהודה's ruling in step 1.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which תנא allows combining two witnesses who give different amounts.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב כהנא himself suggests רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, as shown in the ברייתא that follows.

steps.title: The ברייתא: two separate sets of witnesses are not in dispute
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says בית שמאי and בית הלל agree about two separate sets of witnesses: the smaller amount is included in the larger one.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר said, בית שמאי and בית הלל did not argue about two sets of witnesses, where one set says 100 (a מנה) and the other set says 200, because 100 is included in 200.
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא quotes the source he has in mind. Its first half says everyone agrees about two separate sets of witnesses: they combine for the lower amount.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each set here is a full pair of witnesses. One pair says 200 and one pair says 100, and saying 200 already includes 100. So both pairs back the 100, and everyone agrees it must be paid. This is the easy case, and it prepares for the harder one next.

keyTerms.meaning: Sets (groups) of witnesses, each a full pair

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר:
phrases.english: As it is taught: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: לֹא נֶחְלְקוּ בֵּית שַׁמַּאי וּבֵית הִלֵּל
phrases.english: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel did not disagree
about two sets of witnesses
where one says one hundred,
and one says two hundred,
for two hundred includes one hundred.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּתַנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings the ברייתא that step 2 pointed to.
steps.raayaObject: The idea that a smaller amount is included in a larger amount in testimony.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ברייתא of רבי שמעון בן אלעזר

steps.title: The real dispute: one set of witnesses who disagree
steps.stepSummary: The argument is about two witnesses in one set who give different amounts. בית שמאי say the testimony is split, and בית הלל say 100 is included in 200.
steps.simpleTranslation: What did they argue about? About one set of witnesses, where one witness says 100 and the other says 200. בית שמאי say their testimony is split and does not count. בית הלל say 100 is included in 200.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא now shows the case where בית שמאי and בית הלל really argue: two witnesses in the same pair who give different amounts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here no amount has two witnesses saying it in exactly the same words. בית שמאי say a split testimony is not real testimony. בית הלל still join the two witnesses for 100. This matches רב יהודה's ruling, where two witnesses disagreed (two versus three) and he joined them for two.

keyTerms.meaning: One set (a single pair) of witnesses
Their testimony is split (so it does not count)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two cases. With two full SETS of witnesses, everyone agrees. The argument is only about ONE pair whose two witnesses disagree, and that is רב כהנא's case.

phrases.english: About what did they disagree?
About one set,
where one says one hundred,
and one says two hundred;
for Beit Shammai say: their testimony is divided,
and Beit Hillel say:
two hundred includes one hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the ברייתא by giving the case where the argument really is.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, בית הלל join two disagreeing witnesses of one set for the smaller amount, and בית שמאי do not.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the exact basis רב כהנא thinks רב יהודה relied on, so whether the הלכה follows this ברייתא decides his case.

steps.title: רב כהנא: a letter from ארץ ישראל says the הלכה is not like him
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא challenges the ruling, saying he can bring a letter from ארץ ישראל that the הלכה does not follow רבי שמעון בן אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said to him: But I can bring you a letter from the West (ארץ ישראל) saying the הלכה is not like רבי שמעון בן אלעזר!
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא now attacks the ruling. If the הלכה does not follow רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, then רב יהודה had no basis to join the two witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 2 tied רב יהודה's ruling to one תנא. Now רב כהנא says that תנא's view is rejected in practice. Without it, the two witnesses who disagree cannot be combined, and רב כהנא would owe nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The הלכה is not (like this view)

phrases.english: He said to him: But I can bring you
a letter from the West,
phrases.notes: 'The West' is ארץ ישראל, which lies west of בבל.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן אֶלְעָזָר!
phrases.english: that the halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the source named in steps 2 to 4 to challenge the ruling in step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב יהודה's ruling to pay two rows (step 1).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ruling depends on רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, but ארץ ישראל rules against him, so the ruling has no basis.

steps.title: רב יהודה: bring the letter, and then we will see
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה answers that he will deal with the letter when רב כהנא actually brings it. Until then, his ruling stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said to him: When you bring it, then we will talk.
steps.whatsHappening: רב יהודה does not change his ruling. He tells רב כהנא to first bring the letter he is talking about.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה does not argue with what the letter supposedly says. He only says that a letter nobody has shown him cannot overturn a ruling. So the ruling stays in place, and the גמרא does not say any more about the letter. It moves straight on to a new case.

keyTerms.meaning: When you bring it (then we will see)

steps.whatToRemember: רב יהודה joined two witnesses who disagreed for the smaller amount, following בית הלל as רבי שמעון בן אלעזר explains them. רב כהנא claimed ארץ ישראל rules otherwise, but רב יהודה kept his ruling until proof is actually shown.

phrases.english: He said to him: When you bring it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב כהנא's challenge from step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Puts off the challenge: a claim must be proven before it can overturn the ruling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב כהנא's mention of the letter should be enough to cancel the ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: Until the letter is actually brought, רב יהודה's ruling stands.

steps.title: A man lives in a loft in קשתא, and the old owner comes back
steps.stepSummary: A man has lived in a house for four years. The original owner shows up and objects. The man says he bought it from someone who had bought it from the original owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man lived in a loft in קשתא for four years. The owner of the house came and found him there and asked, 'What are you doing in this house?' The man answered, 'I bought it from so-and-so, who bought it from you.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is telling a story that sets up a court case. It lays out the facts so we can see how רבי חייא rules in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Four years is more than the three years of חזקה, so the man has been living there long enough. The problem is that he never claims he bought it from the owner himself. He says he bought it from a middleman, and the owner never agreed that the middleman owned it.

phrases.english: There was a certain man who lived in קשתא
in a loft, for four years.
The owner of the house came and found him.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: מַאי בָּעֵית בְּהַאי בֵּיתָא?
phrases.english: He said to him: What do you want in this house?
He said to him: I bought it from so-and-so,
who bought it from you.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא, דְּדָר בְּקַשְׁתָּא בְּעִילִּיתָא אַרְבַּע שְׁנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about חזקה through a middleman. It is not connected to the earlier discussion about witnesses.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Facts of the case: four years of living in the house, with a claim of buying it from a middleman.

steps.title: רבי חייא's ruling: show that the seller lived there, even for one day
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא says the buyer keeps the house only if witnesses saw the seller living in it, even for a single day. Without such witnesses, he does not keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The man came before רבי חייא. רבי חייא told him: 'If you have witnesses that the person you bought from lived in the house, even for one day, I will leave it in your hands. If not, I won't.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא rules on the case. The buyer needs witnesses that his seller actually lived in the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the seller was seen living there, that suggests he really owned it, and the buyer's years of living there build on that. Without any sign that the seller was ever there, the buyer's story about a middleman has nothing to support it, so the house goes back to the original owner.

keyTerms.meaning: I will leave it in your possession

steps.whyThisMatters: This ruling is the subject of the rest of the passage. רב questions it, and רבא tries to prove it.

phrases.english: He came before רבי חייא,

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אִי אִית לָךְ סָהֲדֵי
phrases.english: who said to him: If you have witnesses
that the one you bought from lived in it,
even for one day,
I will leave it in your hands;
and if not, then not.
phrases.notes: If there are no witnesses, the house goes back to the original owner.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the court's ruling on the case described in step 7.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The buyer keeps the house only if there are witnesses that his seller lived in it, even for one day.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A buyer who has lived in the house for the חזקה period keeps it only if witnesses saw his seller living there, even for one day. Otherwise the house goes back to the original owner.

steps.title: רב asks: people sometimes buy and sell very quickly
steps.stepSummary: רב, רבי חייא's nephew, questions the ruling. A person could buy a house and resell it right away, before anyone saw him living there.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: I was sitting before my uncle (רבי חייא) and I said to him: 'But don't people sometimes buy and sell in the same night?'
steps.whatsHappening: רב challenges רבי חייא's requirement that the seller must have been seen living in the house.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A real seller might have owned the house for only a short time and never lived in it. If so, requiring witnesses that he lived there seems unfair to an honest buyer.

keyTerms.meaning: My uncle (רב's name for רבי חייא)
Likely to, it is common to

phrases.english: רב said: I was sitting
before my uncle,
phrases.notes: חביבי here means רבי חייא, who was רב's uncle.

phrases.english: and I said to him:
But isn't it common for a person
to buy and sell during the night?
phrases.notes: He means buying and reselling so fast that nobody ever sees the seller living there.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי אֵין אָדָם עָשׂוּי לִיקַּח וְלִמְכּוֹר בַּלַּיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי חייא's ruling from step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי חייא's requirement that the seller must have been seen living in the house
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A real sale can happen so quickly that the seller never lives there. Requiring witnesses that he lived there could cost an honest buyer his house.

steps.title: רבי חייא believes the buyer if he says he saw the sale, because of a מיגו
steps.stepSummary: רב reports what he understood of רבי חייא's view. If the buyer says 'my seller bought it from you in front of me,' he is believed, because he could have claimed something even stronger.
steps.simpleTranslation: I saw that his opinion was this: if the buyer says to the owner, 'The man before me bought it from you in my presence,' he is believed. That is because, if he wanted, he could have said, 'I bought it from you myself.'
steps.whatsHappening: This answers רב's concern. A buyer is not stuck when there are no witnesses, as long as he says he saw the earlier sale with his own eyes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: After three years of living in the house, the buyer would be believed if he said 'I bought it from you.' So he is also believed when he makes the weaker claim that he saw the owner sell it to his seller. This is a מיגו. The case that still fails is a buyer who has no witnesses and does not claim to have seen the sale.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Since' — a person is believed because he could have made a stronger claim

steps.confusionAlert: This does not cancel רבי חייא's ruling. It only adds another way for the buyer to win: claiming he saw the earlier sale himself.

phrases.english: And I saw his opinion,
that if he said to him:
He bought it from you in front of me,
he is believed,
since if he wanted, he could have said to him:
I bought it from you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רב's concern from step 9 by showing a way the buyer can still win.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the ruling: there is a way for the buyer to win even without witnesses
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Without witnesses that the seller lived there, a buyer can never keep the house.
steps.terutzMaskana: If the buyer says he saw the earlier sale happen, he is believed because of a מיגו.

steps.title: רבא supports רבי חייא from the משנה about an heir
steps.stepSummary: רבא says the משנה about an heir backs up רבי חייא. The משנה says an heir does not need a claim, which suggests he still needs proof.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It makes sense to rule like רבי חייא, because the משנה teaches: 'One who comes through inheritance does not need a claim.' He does not need a claim, but he does need proof.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא brings a proof from the משנה to support רבי חייא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An heir does not have to explain how his father got the land. רבא reads the משנה as saying that the heir still needs proof, such as witnesses that his father lived there. In the same way, a buyer needs proof that his seller lived in the house.

keyTerms.meaning: It makes sense, it is reasonable
A claim (explaining how one got ownership)

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רָבָא: כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא מִסְתַּבְּרָא,
phrases.english: רבא said: It makes sense to rule like רבי חייא,
because it is taught: One who comes through inheritance
does not need a claim.
It is a claim that he does not need,
but proof he does need.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: כְּווֹתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא מִסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבי חייא's ruling in step 8 and brings support for it.
steps.raayaObject: רבי חייא's ruling that a buyer needs proof that his seller lived in the house
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה 'הבא משום ירושה אינו צריך טענה', read to mean that proof is still needed

steps.title: Maybe the heir needs neither proof nor a claim
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back on רבא's reading of the משנה. Perhaps an heir needs no proof either.
steps.simpleTranslation: But maybe he does not need proof, and he does not need a claim either!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges how רבא read the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only says the heir does not need a claim. It never says he needs proof. If the heir needs neither, the משנה tells us nothing about requiring proof, and רבא's support for רבי חייא is gone.

phrases.english: But maybe he does not need proof,
and does not need a claim!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְדִלְמָא לָא רְאָיָה בָּעֵי, וְלָא טַעֲנָה בָּעֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the inference רבא made in step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects רבא's reading of the משנה
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה only says no claim is needed. It does not prove that proof is needed.

steps.title: A buyer is different: he does not throw money away
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: even if an heir needs proof, a buyer is different. Nobody pays money without checking first.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say instead: a buyer is different, because he doesn't throw away money for nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another reason why רבא's proof does not work: the heir's case cannot be compared to a buyer's.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if we accept that an heir needs proof, a buyer paid real money, so he must have checked that the seller owned the house. That makes a buyer more trustworthy than an heir, so you cannot learn the buyer's case from the heir's. רבא's proof for רבי חייא's ruling falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (introduces another answer)

steps.whatToRemember: רבי חייא requires witnesses that the seller lived there, though a buyer who says he saw the earlier sale is believed because of a מיגו. רבא tried to prove רבי חייא's ruling from the heir in the משנה. The גמרא rejects that proof two ways: maybe the heir needs no proof, and a buyer, who paid money, is different anyway.

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
A buyer is different,
because he does not throw away money for nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different reason why רבא's proof in step 11 does not work.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the heir's case to decide the buyer's case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: A buyer who paid money surely checked first, so he cannot be compared to an heir.

steps.title: What if the seller was only seen in the house?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask whether seeing the seller in the house is enough to show he owned it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A question was asked: if the seller was only seen in the house, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new open question about what kind of evidence is good enough. This sets up the two answers that come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now, the cases were about witnesses who saw the earlier owner actually living in the house. Here the witnesses only saw him there, maybe just visiting or looking around. The question is whether that weaker sighting still proves he owned it.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was raised before them (the חכמים)
He was seen in it (in the house)

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
If he was seen in it, what is the law?
phrases.notes: "He" is the seller, the person the current owner says he bought the house from.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to רבי חייא's requirement in step 8 and asks whether a weaker kind of evidence, the seller simply being seen in the house, is enough to meet it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does simply seeing the seller in the house count as proof that he owned it?

steps.title: אביי: Being seen there counts
steps.stepSummary: אביי says being seen in the house is the same as living there.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: It is the same thing.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the question. In his view, seeing the seller in the house works just like seeing him live there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For אביי, a person who is seen in a house is assumed to be there as its owner. So this sighting is good enough to back up the buyer's claim.

phrases.english: אביי said:
It is the same thing.
phrases.notes: He means it counts just like witnesses who saw the seller living there.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first answer to the question in step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Being seen in the house counts as proof, the same as living there.

steps.title: רבא: People look at land without buying it
steps.stepSummary: רבא disagrees and says being seen there proves nothing, because people often look at land and don't buy it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: A person often looks over land and does not buy it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the opposite answer to the same question. Seeing the seller in the house does not prove he owned it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא points out that a person may walk around a property to look it over before deciding whether to buy. So being seen there may only mean he was checking it out, not that he bought it.

keyTerms.meaning: A person tends to do (this is normal behavior)

phrases.english: רבא said:
A person tends to look over land
and then not buy it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר: עֲבִיד אִינִישׁ דְּסָיַאר אַרְעֵיהּ וְלָא זָבֵין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to step 14 that disagrees with אביי.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Being seen in the house is not proof, because people often inspect land without buying it.
steps.whatToRemember: אביי: seeing the seller in the house counts as proof. רבא: it does not, since people often look at land and never buy it.

steps.title: Three buyers can combine for a חזקה, only with a שטר
steps.stepSummary: Three buyers in a row can add their years together to make a חזקה, and רב says this works only if each one bought with a שטר.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three buyers combine. רב said: And only if all of them bought with a document.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a rule that three buyers in a row can add up their years to reach the three years of חזקה. רב adds a condition to this rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each buyer held the field for about a year, together they reach three years. רב says this works only when each bought with a שטר, since a written document makes the sale public. Then the original owner should have known about the sales and protested.

keyTerms.meaning: A written document (here, a bill of sale)

phrases.english: Three buyers combine.
phrases.notes: One sells to the next, and together their years of using the field add up to the three years needed for חזקה.

phrases.english: רב said: And all of them with a document.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new rule about חזקה, not connected to the question of אביי and רבא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three buyers in a row combine their years toward a חזקה, but according to רב only if each one bought with a שטר.
steps.whyThisMatters: רב's condition rests on the idea that a שטר makes a sale public. The next step challenges exactly that idea.

steps.title: Don't witnesses also make a sale public?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רב can say only a שטר makes a sale public, when he elsewhere rules that a sale before witnesses creates a lien.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is this to say that רב holds a document makes a sale public, but witnesses do not? But רב said: One who sells a field before witnesses, the buyer collects from sold-off property!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב by comparing this ruling with another ruling of his. The two rulings seem to point in opposite directions.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב's condition suggests that a sale with only witnesses does not become public. But elsewhere רב says a sale before witnesses creates a lien, so the buyer can collect from land the seller later sold to others. That only makes sense if a sale before witnesses does become public, so later buyers knew about it.

keyTerms.meaning: Publicity, "a voice": people hear about it
Property that is tied to a debt but was already sold to others

steps.confusionAlert: In רב's second ruling, the buyer collects because his own field was taken by the seller's creditor. He then takes back his loss from land the seller sold later.

phrases.english: Is this to say that רב holds:
a document makes publicity,
but witnesses do not make publicity?
But didn't רב say:
One who sells a field before witnesses,
he collects from tied-up property that was sold!
phrases.notes: "He" is the buyer. If his field is taken from him, he can collect from land the seller sold to others afterward.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב's condition from step 17 using another ruling of רב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's condition that the buyers must each have a שטר
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Contradiction between two rulings of רב: one implies witnesses don't make a sale public, the other assumes they do.

steps.title: The answer begins: there it is about buyers
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts to answer by pointing out that the other ruling is about buyers, and the answer continues on the next lines.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its answer to the contradiction. The text stops in the middle of the answer, and it continues right after this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer starts by saying the two rulings deal with different people. The ruling about collecting from sold land is about later buyers, unlike the original owner in the חזקה case. The rest of the reason comes in the next lines.

phrases.english: There, buyers
phrases.notes: "There" means רב's ruling about selling before witnesses. The sentence finishes on the next lines.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the contradiction raised in step 18.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing the cases (who needs to know about the sale)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both of רב's rulings are about the same kind of publicity, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer begins by saying the lien ruling is about buyers. The full explanation continues past this point.
